data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism asserts the preference is 'a decision-theoretic choice for maximum information gain, completely orthogonal to inductive probability.' This is internally contradictory. Decision-theoretic reasoning requires a probability distribution over future states to compute expected utility or expected information gain. The target's own claim language—'higher risk and higher potential yield'—is explicitly forward-looking, evaluating what the theory *will* produce, which presupposes probabilistic expectations about future outcomes. One cannot simultaneously frame the choice as decision-theoretic (which is probability-laden by definition) and 'completely orthogonal to inductive probability' (which denies any probabilistic assumption). The target thus undermines its own dissolution: either the choice is genuinely decision-theoretic, in which case it relies on inductive probability and the dilemma is not dissolved, or it is genuinely orthogonal to probability, in which case it is not decision-theoretic and the rationale collapses into mere description. This is a new objection distinct from prior criticisms: objection 2 argued the target sidesteps the induction charge by restating Popperian mechanics, whereas this objection identifies an explicit logical self-contradiction in the target's own framing—decision theory and orthogonality to probability cannot coexist.
